opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. FunSearch came out of a fairly simple observation. When people use AI for scientific discovery, the system often gives you an answer, a number, a structure, a prediction, but not an explanation. For mathematics and computer science, that's unsatisfying. What you really want is something you can inspect, understand, and build on.

Programs are a wonderful representation for that. If you search over programs instead of directly over solutions, the output is a compact description of *how* to build the solution. A program that constructs a large cap set, or a heuristic for bin packing, is often much shorter than the object it produces, and a human can read it and say, "Oh, that's the symmetry it's exploiting." That interpretability turned out to be one of the most valuable parts of the project. Mathematicians could look at what the system found and get new ideas from it.

Then the question is: why LLMs? The search space of programs is enormous, and traditional program synthesis struggled to explore it in a meaningful way. Large language models trained on lots of code carry a strong prior about what reasonable programs look like. So they're very good at proposing plausible variations, essentially creative mutations, of existing code.

But LLMs on their own hallucinate. They'll confidently give you something that's wrong. So the key design choice in FunSearch was pairing the LLM with an automated evaluator. The LLM proposes programs, the evaluator runs them and scores them objectively, and the best ones go back into the prompt to guide the next round. It's an evolutionary loop. The creativity comes from the model, and the rigor comes from the evaluator. That combination lets you go beyond what the model knows and find genuinely new results, like improved constructions for the cap set problem, which was the first time we saw an LLM-based system make a verifiable discovery on an open problem in mathematics.

So in short: programs give you interpretability and compactness, LLMs give you a smart way to search that space, and evaluation keeps the whole thing grounded in truth.

fable-5.1.text:
The honest answer is that it came out of a frustration. We'd had these remarkable successes with systems like AlphaFold and AlphaTensor, but in each case the result was, in a sense, a black box. AlphaTensor would hand you a faster matrix multiplication algorithm as a tensor decomposition, and you could verify it was correct, but you couldn't really read it. You couldn't look at it and say, "Ah, here's the insight." And for a mathematician or a computer scientist, the insight is the whole point. The number is nice, but the understanding is what lets you go further.

So we started asking: what if the thing we search over isn't a solution, but a program that generates the solution? Programs have this wonderful property that they're compact, they're interpretable, and they're compositional. If you find a short program that produces a large cap set, or a good bin-packing heuristic, you can actually read it. A human can look at it, see the structure, and often generalize it to cases the search never touched. That's exactly what happened with the cap set result, where the program revealed a symmetry that led to new constructions.

The second piece was that large language models had, almost as a side effect of being trained on so much code, become quite good at proposing plausible programs. Not correct programs necessarily, but programs that are in the right neighborhood. And that's precisely what you want from a proposal mechanism inside an evolutionary loop. On its own, an LLM will happily hallucinate. But if you pair it with an evaluator that is cheap, automatic, and completely unforgiving, something that just scores the program and throws away the bad ones, then the hallucination problem becomes a feature. You get creativity on one side and rigor on the other.

And I think that pairing is the deeper reason we pursued it. It's a template for how to use these models for discovery safely. The model is never trusted to be right. It's only trusted to be interesting. The verifier decides what's right. So when FunSearch produced something new in mathematics, we weren't relying on the model's confidence, we were relying on a proof-checker, effectively. That felt like the right division of labor, and it's one we've carried forward into a lot of what we've done since.

astra-6.text:
The motivation was to combine the creativity of language models with something we can check rigorously. A language model can propose an interesting idea, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the idea is correct. With a program, we can execute it and evaluate how well it solves the problem. That gives us a feedback signal for the search.

And programs are a very useful space to search in because a short piece of code can describe a strategy that applies to many instances of a problem. Instead of asking the model for one answer, you’re asking it to discover a procedure for producing good answers.

So in FunSearch, the model proposes programs, an evaluator tests them, and the successful ones become the starting point for further proposals. You get this iterative process where the model’s creativity is guided by reliable evaluation. And the result is code that researchers can inspect, which gives them a chance to understand why a particular strategy works and extract a new idea from it.

sol-6.1.text:
The motivation was to combine the creativity of large language models with the rigor of computation. A model can propose an interesting idea, but that doesn’t mean the idea is correct. With a program, we can actually run it and evaluate whether it does what we want—and whether it improves on what we already have.

That gives you a feedback loop. The language model proposes programs, we evaluate them, and the best ones become examples for the next round of proposals. You’re searching over a space of possible solutions, guided by an objective measure of quality.

And a program is more than an answer to a single instance. It can encode a strategy that works across many instances. You can inspect it, try to understand why it works, and potentially extract a new mathematical insight. That combination—creative proposals, reliable evaluation, and an interpretable result—was what made the approach so appealing.
